title: What is known about 1RB1RC_1LC1LC_1RE0LD_1LB1RF_---1RA_0RD1RD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1RC_1LC1LC_1RE0LD_1LB1RF_---1RA_0RD1RD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open, and reduced to a map. Lean's kernel proves that the machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of an explicit map on two counts reaches u = v or u = v + 1, and that the first 10,000 rounds do not; the map iterated for 106 rounds does not get there, and a probability argument says it never will.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (E0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 34,174 cells have been visited and 34,170 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: exp/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.058). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.5).

claims.title: Every round, in closed form
claims.text: For every u ≥ 3 and v, from the round start P u v = C> 0 11 0 (11)^u 0 (11)^v (or Q u v, with one more 11 0) the machine reaches the next round start given by the map next: P u v → P(3u+2, v−u−1) if u < v, → Q(3v+3, u−v−2) if u ≥ v+2; Q u v → Q(3u+3, v−u−1) or P(3v+5, u−v−2); and it halts if u = v or u = v + 1. Built from 31 symbolic rules and an induction on the number of bounces.

claims.title: Halting reduced to the map
claims.text: The machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of next from P 3 0 (reached in 42 steps) reaches a pair with u = v or u = v + 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 rounds
claims.text: The map, evaluated by the kernel, does not reach the diagonal in 10,000 rounds; the counts then have about 3,000 bits, far beyond any simulated step count.

claims.title: No halt in the first 3·10<sup>6</sup> rounds
claims.text: The map iterated with Python integers for 3·106 rounds does not reach the diagonal; u + v grows by about 0.307 bits a round. The first round starts of a direct simulation agree with the map.

claims.title: Why it is expected never to halt
claims.text: The ratio u/(u+v) moves like a chaotic orbit of an expanding map, so a round lands within one of the diagonal with chance about 1/(u+v), which shrinks geometrically; the total chance of a halt after the computed rounds is about 2−900000. No congruence excludes the diagonal (the residues reachable mod m include diagonal ones for every m tried).

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known: it halts iff the subtract-and-triple orbit ever brings the two counts within one of each other. A cryptid in the bbchallenge sense.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, but the question is now a small arithmetic one. This machine plays a game with two numbers: subtract the smaller from the larger, triple the smaller, repeat. It stops only if the two numbers ever come within one of each other. Lean proves that this is exactly what the machine does; the numbers have been followed for three million rounds.

facts.text: Halting reduced to a two-counter map, proved in Lean.
The map, iterated without reaching the diagonal.
Chance of a halt still to come, by a random model.

sections.heading: Two blocks and a counter of rounds
html: Count cells in pairs. At the start of every round the head is in state C on the blank cell left of the tape, and the tape is one of

with a middle block of u pairs and a last block of v pairs. The head runs right, then bounces: it walks back into the middle block and returns to the right end, and each bounce takes a pair off the middle block, a pair off the last block and adds three pairs to the block on the left. When the smaller block is used up the head walks to the left end and the next round starts: the block on the left becomes the new middle block, the rest of the larger block the new last block.

A round costs about (u+v)·min(u,v) steps, so the blocks (the right part of the tape) grow like the square root of the step count, while each round adds a few cells at the left end: that side grows like the logarithm. That is the exp/sqrt shape of the run.

The halt: when both blocks run out in the same bounce, the head runs off the right end in state E, which has no transition on a blank cell. From blank tape the machine reaches P 3 0 after 42 steps, and then:
Round 1 came close: Q 3 1 has u − v = 2, one more than a halting difference. In Lean: next, round and round_halt in lean/Macro.lean, and halts_iff' in lean/Reduction.lean.

sections.heading: Only if the two numbers meet
html: The machine halts iff some round has u = v or u = v + 1. Lean's kernel proves that equivalence and that the first 10,000 rounds stay off the diagonal; Python follows the map for 106 rounds, when u + v has about 92,000 digits.

Why nobody expects a halt: the share u/(u+v) moves chaotically (below one half it goes to 3x/(1+x), above it to the mirror image), so landing within one of the diagonal has a chance of about one in u + v, and u + v grows by about a quarter every round. The chances add up to almost nothing. But no argument rules it out: the counts are not prevented from meeting by any congruence, so a proof would need to control the order of the counts, as for the Collatz-like cryptids.

html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the logarithm of the step count: each new cell costs a roughly constant factor more time, the signature of a counter or of a Collatz-like map whose values are written on the tape (fitted exponent 0.058). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.5).
After 109 steps the tape spans 34,174 cells (67 left of the start, 23,197 right), with a density of 1s of 1.0.

summary: Halts iff a two-counter map (subtract the smaller count from the larger and triple it) lands on its diagonal; reduction proved in Lean, no hit in 10<sup>6</sup> rounds.
